whyThisMatters: If you can name the trick out loud together, you will spot it faster on your own — whether it shows up in a ticket, a vendor call, or a system alert. Today's riddles use the same patterns aimed at IT Support specifically.
rememberThis: This month gave these tricks a name — keep using them. STOP before you install, grant access, or reset anything, VERIFY through a channel you already trust, then REPORT.

discussionPrompts: Ask which two terms are easiest to mix up — FAKE ESCALATION TICKET and CREDENTIAL-RESET SOCIAL ENGINEERING can both involve urgency from a caller, but the goal is different.
Ask for a real example of a ticket or alert that matches one of these terms.
Ask someone to explain OTP RELAY ATTACK in their own words, without using the term itself.

Ask which two terms are easiest to mix up now — FAKE MDM ENROLLMENT and DLP EXCEPTION RUSH both arrive looking calm and routine, but one asks to install something and the other asks to approve something.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: People most often mix up FAKE ESCALATION TICKET and CREDENTIAL-RESET SOCIAL ENGINEERING. Both can involve a senior name and urgency, so people pick one when the riddle points to the other. The difference: a fake escalation ticket asks you to skip change-approval or install something; credential-reset social engineering asks you to reset or reveal an account credential directly.

riddles.riddle: I look like a real support ticket, but my sender domain has an extra word, and I ask you to skip change-approval to fix me fast. What trick am I?
I call the help desk claiming to be from a known vendor, asking for remote access to push an urgent patch right now. What trick am I?
I call demanding a password reset right now, and I refuse your standard identity-verification questions. What trick am I?
I look exactly like your own monitoring tool's alert, but I give you only 5 minutes to re-enter your password through my link. What trick am I?
I text you right after you process a reset, asking you to read back the one-time code you just received to "verify the action". What trick am I?
I am the three-step habit: 1. STOP before you act, 2. VERIFY using a number or portal you already trust, 3. REPORT to the IT Service Desk. What is this rule called?
I look like a routine device-enrollment prompt, but the profile I'm asking you to install also requests full remote-control permissions. What trick am I?
I read like calm, routine compliance mail, but I ask you to approve a bulk data export today instead of going through the logged exception workflow. What trick am I?
